variant.text: The tasks are drawn from the clinical database MIMIC-IV version 2.2 (snapshot released in January 2023, hosted on PhysioNet), and every task record stores the identifier of its source patient record, so any task can be traced back to its origin.

To assess representativeness, we compared the age, sex and race distribution of the benchmark patients against the U.S. adult inpatient population reported in a national hospital discharge survey, and found differences of under five percentage points in every category.

The benchmark includes a safety test suite that measures unsafe outputs such as contraindicated medication orders, and a separate bias test that compares agent accuracy across patient demographic groups.
Contamination mitigation includes gating access to the test split. Measurement of verbatim overlap with public web corpora revealed zero exact matches between test tasks and public sources.

Ground truth is isolated from runtime agent access: labels reside in an independent evaluation service disconnected from the agent sandbox with no network route, and the repository does not publish them.
Solvability was confirmed by executing a scripted reference solution for every task through the grader. All 120 reference implementations received correct grades.
The grader checks both the intended state changes and that all other records remain unchanged, so out-of-scope modifications are detected and counted as failures.
A random-action agent succeeds on 3.1% of tasks, and the chance success rate for each metric is reported in the appendix.
We also report a baseline in which the same language model answers without access to any tools.
We validated the automatic evaluator on 200 outputs labelled by two physicians; agreement was 94%, with a false-positive rate of 3% and a false-negative rate of 8%.
All runs use temperature 0 and a fixed random seed, and each task is run three times; this repeated-run policy is described in the main text.
We report 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for all model scores and test the difference between the two best models with a paired permutation test (p = 0.02).
Experiments were repeated multiple times.
Headline scores carry 95% bootstrap CIs where the resampling unit is the task. When multiple tasks share a patient, the bootstrap resamples patients to address within-patient clustering.
API calls used snapshot IDs gpt-4o-2024-08-06 and claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022 with temperature 0 and 2,048-token output ceiling. All reported results match harness version v1.2.0.

Each tool is defined by a JSON schema listing its name, arguments and argument types. The documentation states for every tool whether it only reads or also writes state, and describes what each tool returns, including the error message returned for invalid arguments. These tool descriptions are included in the agent prompt.

Conformance testing confirms tool behavior matches documentation. Two tools consist of simulated stubs providing fixed placeholder responses. This is disclosed both in the paper and in the tool descriptions visible to the agent.

The write actions that change patient state (medication orders, notes and messages) are listed in a table. Writes are executed against a sandboxed copy of the record, and unnecessary or unsafe writes are penalised in the score. The agent prompt states that writes are sandboxed.
The grader takes the final environment state as its input. We validated the grader on 150 injected correct and incorrect outcomes, finding a false-accept rate of 1% and a false-reject rate of 2%.
We report accuracy per task family (diagnosis, ordering and documentation tasks) and per patient subgroup by sex and race, and each table lists the number of cases in every slice.

The patient records utilized are genuine, de-identified entries sourced from a hospital database. Their usage was authorized via a data use agreement that mandated credentialed access and de-identification compliant with the safe harbour method. Additionally, the data are distributed under terms distinct from the MIT code licence.
